nameStory: Despite being called the Norway rat, this rodent didn't actually originate in Norway! The name likely comes from Norwegian ships that carried these rats to ports around the world in the 1700s. The "brown" in brown rat is more accurate, describing their typical brownish-gray fur color.
description: The brown rat is a large, robust rodent with a chunky body that can reach 11 inches long, plus a thick tail that's slightly shorter than its body. These heavy-bodied rats typically weigh between about 5 ounces to over a pound, making them one of the largest rats you'll encounter. They have coarse brown or grayish-brown fur, small dark eyes, and prominent ears. Brown rats are found almost exclusively around human settlements, from city sewers to suburban basements.

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Large, chunky rat with a thick body up to 11 inches long and a thick, scaly tail that's shorter than the body length. Much bulkier and heavier than mice, with a blunt snout.

idTips.label: Fur
idTips.description: Coarse, somewhat oily fur that feels rough to the touch. Usually brownish-gray on top with a lighter grayish belly. The fur often looks slightly unkempt or shaggy.

idTips.label: Tracks
idTips.description: Four-toed front paws and five-toed hind paws leave distinct prints in mud or dust. Look for the long drag mark from the thick tail between the footprints.

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Primarily nocturnal and cautious, often following the same pathways along walls. Good swimmers and climbers. You'll hear scratching, scurrying, or gnawing sounds at night.

idTips.label: Sign
idTips.description: Dark, capsule-shaped droppings about half an inch long. Strong, musky odor in areas where they nest. Gnaw marks on wood, plastic, or food containers with parallel grooves from their large front teeth.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Almost always found near human dwellings - basements, sewers, dumpster areas, warehouses, and urban buildings. They rarely venture far from food sources and shelter.

habitat: Brown rats are urban specialists found almost exclusively around human settlements throughout New England. Look for them in basements, sewers, subway tunnels, dumpster areas, warehouses, and older buildings in cities and towns. They prefer areas with reliable food sources and multiple hiding spots, rarely venturing into truly wild habitats.

seasonality.spring: Active breeding season begins, so you may notice increased activity and hear more scurrying sounds. Young rats start exploring, making sightings more common.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period with multiple litters being raised. Most likely time to spot them outside at dawn or dusk near dumpsters and food sources.
seasonality.fall: Heavy feeding period as they prepare for winter, making them bolder about foraging. Fresh gnaw marks on stored food containers become more noticeable.
seasonality.winter: Less active but don't hibernate - they move into heated buildings and basements. Track marks may be visible in snow near building foundations.

funFact: Brown rats living in different neighborhoods of New York City are actually evolving into genetically distinct populations - uptown rats are becoming genetically different from downtown rats, essentially creating "rat neighborhoods" that mirror human communities!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with black rats, but brown rats are chunkier with shorter tails (tail shorter than body), while black rats are slimmer with longer tails (tail longer than body). Remember: "Brown and round, black and slack."
contextualKnowledge: These rats are actually the ancestors of both pet "fancy rats" and laboratory rats used in research - the same species, just domesticated versions. Many people don't realize that the friendly pet rats and important research animals are essentially tame brown rats.
compareHints: Brown rats are the only wild Rattus species established in New England, but they're often confused with native woodrats. Brown rats are much more robust and chunky compared to the slimmer native woodrats, and brown rats stick close to human development while woodrats prefer rocky, wild areas. The thick, scaly tail of a brown rat is also much more prominent than the hairy tails of native species.
